sections.title: Rubber compound options
sections.chip: 🛑 SBR crazes in sun · EPDM missing
sections.live: LIVE → Neoprene, SBR — two of the eight, presented as equals · EPDM, the automotive glazing standard, is not offered

fields.label: All eight, always — and this page has a live selection error
paragraphs: Margo produces every part in every compound it mixes (client-instructed 2026-09-02). The live selector offers two, which understates the offer by six.

🛑 Worse, one of the two is wrong for the duty. SBR has poor ozone resistance. This part sits on the outside of the vehicle in direct sunlight for the life of the car, and ozone attack on a stressed rubber surface produces exactly the fine cracking that makes an old windscreen rubber perish. A buyer choosing SBR from an unranked list of two gets a part that crazes.

And the right answer is absent. EPDM is the universal automotive glazing compound — weatherstrips, glass runs, door seals — precisely because it resists ozone and UV and stays flexible cold. It is not on this page.

fields.label: Cards ×4
rows: Ozone is what kills a window rubber
Not sunlight and not water — ozone attacking a rubber held in permanent tension. EPDM resists it; the compounds this page currently offers do not.
Sized to the glass and the flange
The seal is interference between glass, rubber and aperture flange. Send all three, or a length of the old rubber — a channel cut for 4 mm glass leaks on 3.8 mm.
Rubber-glazed glass floats in its channel instead of becoming a structural member — which is why ladder-frame vehicles use it. The rubber has to stay compliant cold to keep doing that job.
Section die designed and cut here, profile extruded to length, corners moulded or vulcanised to your drawing. No external toolmaker and no split responsibility for the joint.
fields.note:
Four cards, four cards — no count change and no new element. Each live card is a title plus one line and the replacement keeps that shape exactly.
The four live titles are identical on all 31 pages and would sit unchanged on an oil seal or a floor mat. This is the only block that can carry a per-part argument.
Card 03 is the one worth having. Almost no supplier page explains why a vehicle uses rubber glazing rather than bonded glass, and it is the reason this part exists on a Bolero-class platform at all.
Card 04 is the differentiator — in-house die making is the extrusion equivalent of in-house tooling, and it is genuinely uncommon

notes: This is the page’s AEO asset. Everything else is shared with 30 other URLs.

🛑 Moulding process, named per part: extruded, not compression moulded. The template says compression moulding on all 31 pages — on this part it is simply the wrong process, and a glazing buyer will notice.

sections.title: From compound to certification
sections.chip: Step 03 is the wrong process for this part
sections.live: LIVE H2 → From Compound to Certification · six steps · step 03 says “Compression Moulding”; this part is extruded

fields.label: Steps
rows: Material compounding — polymer blending, additive integration and batch QC in our in-house lab. The weathering package is set here — a glazing profile sits in direct sunlight for the life of the vehicle.
Die design & cutting — extrusion dies designed and cut in-house and held as a controlled record.
Extrusion — continuous profile at controlled temperature and line speed.
Cure, cut and corner-mould — continuous vulcanisation, cut to length, corners moulded or vulcanised into a closed frame.
Quality inspection — section profile check against the drawing, hardness testing and batch sampling before release.

Export packaging — coiled or cut-length packing with documentation. Glazing profiles are coiled to a minimum diameter and never folded — a kink will not seat against the glass. ISPM-15 treated pallets where timber packaging is used.
fields.note:
Six steps, six kept — but four of them need the extrusion vocabulary. This is the clearest case in the catalogue of a shared component describing the wrong process: the live page tells a glazing buyer their profile will be compression moulded, which is not how any glazing rubber has ever been made.
Step 02 remains the strongest line either way — tooling designed and held in-house is the claim that separates a manufacturer from a trader, and it is as true of a die as of a mould

notes: The process block must render from the part record, not from a single hard-coded string. Three processes exist — injection, compression, transfer — plus extrusion, and the template names one.
Numbered steps are an <ol>.
“Continuous vulcanisation” and “corner moulding” are searched terms among glazing buyers and appear nowhere on this site.
